Bahrain runs into the buzzsaw of US war, reacts predictably
item.description:
On Monday, the High Criminal Court in Bahrain’s capital, Manama, sentenced dozens of Shiite clerics to life in prison, on allegations that they “communicated with..and had collected and received funds” from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

As the trial was running its course, Iranian drones were targeting U.S. military installations in Bahrain, with attacks taking place on Friday, Sunday, and again on Tuesday and Wednesday, ending a two-month lull.

Bahrain, the small island kingdom on the eastern side of the Arabian Peninsula, is where the pressures of the U.S.-Iran war are concentrated most tightly. A majority Shia population run by a Sunni ruling family, Bahrain has a current population of 1.6 million people (fewer than half, about 740,000 are citizens; the rest are largely migrant workers, mainly from South Asia) and is home to the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet. It signed the Abraham Accords with Israel, and is also a deeply indebted nation, dependent on its wealthier neighbors for its survival.

This is a volatile mix, and Washington has spent the last nine months, through its war on Iran, piling the pressure on its most vulnerable ally in the region.

Bahrain was ruled from the Persian side of the Gulf for long stretches of its history until 1783, when the Al Khalifa, a Sunni Arab clan from what is today Qatar, took the island and expelled the Iranian-installed governor. Their descendants now form the royal family that rules Bahrain.

Iran, however, never quite accepted this arrangement. Its parliament declared Bahrain the country’s fourteenth province in 1957, and only in 1970, after a U.N. survey found Bahrainis overwhelmingly wanted independence, did the Shah of Iran drop the claim.

The Islamic Republic that now governs Iran has not entirely let go of the past. In April, Kayhan, the Tehran daily whose editor was appointed by the late supreme leader, ran a column declaring that “Bahrain was and is part of Iranian territory.” Hossein Shariatmadari, Kayhan’s managing editor, went on to characterize the ruling family as “puppets of the British government” and accused Bahrain of direct participation in American military attacks on Iran.

The last claim reflects the official government line: Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei defended Iran’s attacks on Bahrain this week, claiming that countries in the region aided American forces, and that Tehran’s strikes were “purely defensive in nature.”

While annexation of Bahrain is not Iranian policy, irredentist rhetoric from hardliners in Tehran has become useful to Bahrain’s leadership, who leverage these threats to frame dissident citizens as a potential fifth column.

As Bahrain’s demographics make clear, it is structurally distinct from its oil-rich, Sunni majority Arab Gulf neighbors. It ran out of meaningful oil reserves long ago and never had the revenue to buy the loyalty of its population. Instead, what it has done is direct a large share of state employment and patronage to its Sunni tribal base, while its Shiite citizens, who make up 55 to 62 percent of the population, are largely excluded from the military and security apparatus where the overwhelming majority of officers are Sunni (many are naturalized foreign-born recruits), and live in underserved neighborhoods and villages.

The fear of Iran is the glue that holds this system together, and that fear is not totally imagined. Bahrain’s government said it foiled a coup attempt in 1981 by a Tehran-linked group known as the Islamic Front for the Liberation of Bahrain. Grand Ayatollah Isa Qassim, the kingdom's most senior Shiite cleric, who was stripped of Bahraini nationality in 2016 and sentenced to life imprisonment in absentia on Monday, has lived in Iran since 2018. Manama also accuses other exiles living there of directing armed attacks on Bahraini police.

But the same fear has also become a convenient justification for Bahrain’s rulers to treat nearly all dissent, including through peaceful means, as treasonous and Iran-backed. This is what happened in 2011, when the Arab Spring came to Bahrain, and a protest movement that included both sects was crushed with the help of Saudi and Emirati troops. Bahrain’s King Hamad used the episode to hint at Iranian involvement.

The same is happening again now. Since the U.S. and Israel initiated hostilities against Iran on February 28, Tehran has retaliated against every Gulf state hosting American forces. Bahrain has, as a result, absorbed hundreds of missiles and drones, which not only struck the Navy’s Fifth Fleet headquarters, but also industrial and residential sites, and a desalination plant.

What made Bahrain’s leadership especially nervous was how some Bahrainis publicly mourned Iran’s slain supreme leader Ali Khamenei, who was killed in the opening blows of the war.

What followed was a crackdown that swept more than 700 people, for filming attacks, and for social media activity deemed anti-government or pro-Iran. In April, the government stripped 69 citizens of their nationality for “glorifying or sympathising with the hostile Iranian acts” and postponed parliamentary elections.

In May and June, Bahraini authorities arrested more than 50 clerics, whose sentences were handed down on Monday.

Within the first 24 hours of that verdict, Iran’s foreign ministry and Qais al-Khazali, the leader of an Iran-backed Iraqi militia, issued statements assailing the trials and sentences. In rushing to defend Bahraini clerics, Iran and its allies hand Manama what looks to it like proof that the convicted answer to foreign patrons, which then fuels harsher repressive measures, and so the cycle continues.

The economic picture for Manama is also dire. Before the war, the International Monetary Fund had put Bahrain's government debt at 134 percent of GDP, among the highest in the world. It is also the only Gulf Cooperative Council state rated “junk” by all three credit agencies, meaning investors view its bonds as high-risk and demand high interest rates to lend its government money. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran has cut off nearly all of its modest oil exports and forced its aluminum smelter, the Gulf’s largest, to declare force majeure.

Bahrain has been bailed out before, by Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Kuwait to the tune of $10 billion in 2018. It will likely be bailed out again, but this time, its primary donor is strained. Saudi Arabia is fighting its own war with the Houthis in Yemen who have hit Riyadh’s airport and business center, and its critical East-West pipeline, which moves roughly four million barrels of crude per day from the Gulf to the Red Sea.

Riyadh is also running a deficit currently projected at $65 billion dollars, up from the $44 billion planned in January, which makes the contours of any future bailout hard to predict.

Whatever form that rescue takes, it will certainly come with strings. Given Bahrain's size and its modest economic means, its freedom of action is limited and it has typically followed the lead of its larger neighbors when it comes to foreign policy.

Before the war, Bahrain was pursuing rapprochement with the Islamic Republic. Despite being one of the inaugural signers of the Abraham Accords with Israel in 2020, it reopened channels with Tehran in 2024, prompted in part by the Saudi-Iranian détente that China brokered in 2023. The current war sealed that opening shut, and now Manama has little room to negotiate with Iran on its own until a wider settlement is worked out.

Yet rather than holding out for diplomacy, Bahrain has taken a more assertive line, using its seat as a non-permanent member of the U.N. Security Council to push resolutions demanding Iran reopen the Strait and stop its attacks on its neighbors. One was adopted in March and later one, which initially contained language authorizing the use of force, was vetoed by Russia and China, who argued it was one-sided for ignoring U.S. and Israeli strikes that provoked Iran’s reaction.

These moves are unlikely to have endeared the kingdom to Tehran, and may also help in understanding why Bahrain has remained in Iran’s crosshairs.

item.title: Trump’s honeymoon with South Korea is over
item.description:
Following his visit to the White House to meet with President Donald Trump in August of last year, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung had good reasons to believe the strategic alliance was in strong shape.

Despite their ideological disagreements, the two leaders held a cordial first summit that in subsequent months led to a resolution of their trade frictions, a $150 billion investment in shipbuilding, substantial investment in commercial projects in the United States, and even a surprise announcement that Trump would help Seoul build nuclear-powered submarines. One of Lee’s key commitments was to increase South Korean defense spending to 3.5% of GDP — the Trump administration’s minimum target for Asian nations.

But what a difference a year can make with Trump. On October 21, U.S. Ambassador to South Korea Michelle Steel publicly described the relationship as experiencing “turbulence.” Lee’s government, for its part, has tried to downplay recent tensions, arguing that overheated domestic politics in both countries need not undermine the strong foundation of the alliance. As South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun told Parliament in late October, “When you’re in turbulence, fasten your seat belt and it won’t be a problem.”

In truth, some of the turbulence is of Seoul’s own making. In March, for example, South Korean Unification Minister Chung Dong-young publicly identified a North Korean uranium enrichment facility, potentially compromising sensitive sources and methods. The Lee government insists that the information was already public, but Washington disagrees and has retaliated by restricting certain satellite-derived intelligence about North Korea and excluded Seoul from a trilateral meeting on North Korean cyber threats.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has complained about intelligence sharing broadly with Seoul, and South Korean Ambassador Kang Kyung-wha acknowledged as recently as last month that his government had not fully addressed Washington’s concerns.

South Korea has also been slow in deciding how to invest its pledged $350 billion, angering Trump in the process. For instance, Trump wants Seoul to invest roughly $54 billion in the Alaska LNG pipeline project, but Lee’s government has questioned its commercial viability. Although he has expressed confidence that South Korea will eventually follow through, Trump has made vague threats to resume tariffs if the deals remain stalled.

Separately, South Korean regulators imposed a fine of $423 million on Coupang, a U.S.-listed e-commerce company, following a massive consumer data breach. The Trump administration and congressional Republicans were outraged by the move, calling it discrimination against American companies, while the Lee administration justified the measure to protect consumer privacy data.

But the Trump administration shares much of the blame for the increasingly contentious bilateral relationship. For one thing, even though Washington and Seoul already agreed in June 2025 to reduce tariffs from 25% to 15% in 2025, Trump periodically threatens to raise tariff rates again to 25% when he gets angry about something. This has surprised and frustrated South Korean officials, who may no longer see Washington as a reliable strategic ally. And perhaps neither do the South Korean people. According to a Pew Research survey from August, 55% of them hold an unfavorable view of the United States — the highest such mark in more than 20 years.

North Korea poses a bilateral challenge as well. To be sure, both Trump and Lee want to prioritize renewed engagement with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un rather than deterrence. But the Trump administration’s preferred approach differs from Seoul’s. Trump surprised South Korea by shortening the annual bilateral military drills, known as Ulchi Freedom Guardian, just hours before they began. He argued that they were unnecessarily provocative toward Kim, whom Trump hopes will join him in a summit.

Although he publicly accepted Trump’s decision to cut back combined military exercises, Lee would rather derive diplomatic leverage from enhanced military preparedness against North Korea, and the deterrence that comes with it, prior to negotiations. Trump further blamed South Korea for not contributing to the U.S. naval operation to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, in turn questioning why Washington continues to defend South Korea on the peninsula.

Deepening disagreements over China represent yet another irritant. The Trump administration clearly seeks greater “flexibility” in how it uses the approximately 28,500 U.S. troops deployed to South Korea. Rather than focusing exclusively on North Korea, Washington has publicly intimated that China could be the target of their future military operations, and that Seoul would be expected to support that mission.

Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge “Bridge” Colby, for example, visited Seoul in January and gave a speech at the Sejong Institute that curiously did not mention North Korea at all, and instead, replaced it with multiple references to countering China. To the shock of South Korean officials, Trump’s National Security Strategy, released last November, neglected to mention North Korea either and focused instead on the need for South Korea to help the U.S. and Japan secure the First Island Chain — a clear reference to containing China. Although Trump’s National Defense Strategy from January did reference North Korea, it avoided stating that denuclearization was still a U.S. priority and put the responsibility to deal with the regime more squarely on Seoul, with limited American support.

Trump’s submarine and shipbuilding deals are also in limbo. On the submarines, Trump wants them built at the South Korean defense firm Hanwha’s shipyard in Philadelphia, but the Lee government argues that South Korea offers more appropriate shipyards because they are already outfitted with advanced submarine-building capabilities. There is also the question surrounding the enriched nuclear fuel and associated sensitive technologies, which Seoul wants Washington to provide. But rules governing the bilateral relationship currently do not permit such transfers without specific exemptions or additional authorizations.

When the submarine deal was first announced in October 2025, none of these issues had been properly considered by the Trump administration, provoking the current disputes. And on broader shipbuilding, South Korea’s $150 billion financial commitment has largely stalled. Indeed, the president’s Make American Shipbuilding Great Again (MASGA) initiative has yielded zero concrete projects, embarrassing Trump, who wants to reenergize the U.S. defense industrial base and add manufacturing jobs. Progress on MASGA has also been hampered by a mix of legal, political, and financial obstacles.

Finally, the fallout from the September 2025 ICE raids on South Korean workers at the Hyundai-LG battery plant in the United States continues. Although Seoul wrapped up its internal investigation without retaliating against the U.S. government, attorneys representing more than 300 of the workers, who were allegedly shackled and abused during the ordeal, are now pursuing administrative damages, possibly a precursor to civil lawsuits, against the Department of Justice, the Department of Homeland Security, the FBI, and others. The political rhetoric surrounding the case became heated on both sides as the legal process continues to unfold.

Despite the growing tensions between them, South Korea and the U.S. remain staunch allies, and in fact, the Trump administration has referred to Seoul as a “model ally,” especially because of its increased defense spending. Lee and Trump reportedly spoke about future diplomatic engagements on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China this week. But difficulties remain, and the next two years under Trump and Lee could prove even more turbulent when it comes to trade, investment, military cooperation, and foreign policy.

Additionally, while many have interpreted the midterm elections as a rebuke of Trump’s foreign policy, they are unlikely to affect U.S.-Korea relations in substantive ways. The president typically has the lead on foreign policy, and lame-duck presidents tend to intensify their focus on it to secure their legacy. item.description:
Nvidia’s former CEO, Jensen Huang, and his extramarital relationship with the alleged Chinese agent Alice Huang, likely will be discussed at the scheduled meeting of President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the 2026 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, China on November 18-19.

It is alleged that Ms. Huang, Managing Director of MegaSpeed International in Singapore and a cloud partner with Nvidia in the Asia-Pacific region, was an agent of China’s Ministry of State Security. She allegedly was part of a “honey trap” operation against Jensen Huang. It is alleged that her company, MegaSpeed , purchased billions of dollars of advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) chips and servers, and in violation of U.S. export-control restrictions, smuggled these advanced AI chips to China.

A spokesperson at China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the allegation that Ms. Huang was a Chinese agent is “baseless” and “slanderous”.

Mr. Trump reportedly said he will not address this issue in his meeting with Mr. Xi, although it is likely that Mr. Xi will address these allegations. Neither the U.S. nor Singapore has filed criminal charges against Ms. Huang, and the Department of Justice said it is looking into the matter without reaching any formal conclusions. It is likely that Congress will conduct hearings related to these allegations.

Both leaders are scheduled to will meet on the margins of the APEC Leaders’ meeting. Russia’s President Vladimir Putin will also attend the APEC session and meet with Presidents Trump and Xi – the first-ever trilateral meeting on the sideline of APEC.

This will be third meeting of Presidents Trump and Xi this year, with a fourth meeting scheduled for December 14 to 15, 2026, at the G20 Leaders’ Summit in Miami, Florida.

Although a formal agenda for the trilateral meeting has not been published, it is likely the three leaders will discuss the wars in Ukraine and Iran, with some discussion of North Korea and its nuclear and missile programs. Both China and Russia have a close allied relationship with Pyongyang. They can – if they want – use their relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un to attempt to convince him to meet for a fourth time with Mr. Trump.

Working-level teams from the three countries reportedly have been negotiating an agenda covering AI in critical weapons systems and a potential joint statement against nuclear war.

Nuclear proliferation is another subject the three leaders will discuss, with the U.S. continuing to encourage China to agree to greater transparency on their nuclear program and an eventual arms control agreement. Previously, China refused to discuss their nuclear program, noting that the U.S. and Russia had significantly more nuclear warheads than China. Once parity in the number of nuclear warheads is reached, China said they would then consider discussing their nuclear program with the U.S.

At the APEC conference, AI and the Digital Economies will be discussed, with emphasis on narrowing the regional digital divide and discussing cross-border digital trade interoperability. Work force reskilling and aligning AI with the energy infrastructure were subjects previously discussed at APEC Ministerial talks.

And given global economic fragmentation and rising costs, officials will prioritize cross-border supply chain stability and interoperability across different national regulatory systems. China is also highlighting regional connectivity through the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao greater bay area initiative.

The APEC meeting will also discuss the green-digital transition, clean energy, food security, and ocean and fisheries sustainability in the Asia-Pacific region.

Regional trade and economic integration will also be discussed, given that 2026 marks the 20th anniversary of the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific vision, that focused on multilateral trade and reducing tariffs.

This APEC meeting will be impactful, given the participation of Presidents Trump, Xi, and Putin.

item.description:
The first trilateral meeting of Presidents Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin, held on November 19 in Shenzhen, was worth holding for one reason above all. The United States has a clear interest in reducing nuclear risks with both China and Russia, and the three leaders agreed to discuss how to do so.

Beyond that, the summit yielded little for Washington. Xi gained the prestige of convening the three powers, while Putin gained stature on the world stage even as Russia continues its brutal war against Ukraine.

The nuclear pledge deserves attention, however. Beijing has long resisted three-way arms-control negotiations, arguing that the United States and Russia should first reduce their much larger arsenals. China has discussed nuclear risks with both countries in the broader five-power process and held bilateral arms-control consultations with Washington in 2023. Beijing suspended further consultations in 2024, citing U.S. arms sales to Taiwan. What Shenzhen adds is Xi’s public commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and nonproliferation in a dedicated three-way format. That is a meaningful opening, especially since New START expired in February.

However, the joint declaration sets no timetable or agenda and contains no commitment to negotiate limits on arsenals.

The other results of the summit were thinner. The leaders endorsed U.N. reform and greater supplies of refined petroleum products without specifying what reforms they wanted or how much additional fuel they would supply. Beijing says they discussed Ukraine, the Middle East, and the Korean Peninsula, but the declaration identified no concrete next steps. Its language on immunity for state officials and alleged jurisdictional abuse by the International Criminal Court (ICC) had a clearer political payoff. It aligned with the Trump administration’s position and benefited Putin, who faces an ICC arrest warrant.

Xi also brought a familiar proposal into the three-way meeting by calling for crisis communication and prevention mechanisms. Although the joint declaration contained no agreement to establish them, Washington and Moscow should nevertheless take up the proposal and see whether Beijing will agree to practical steps, such as establishing and regularly testing emergency contacts.

On balance, Shenzhen was long on symbolism and promises and short on results that advance global stability or U.S. interests. That judgment could change if the three governments schedule nuclear talks and agree on measures that reduce the risk of miscalculation. The summit gave them an opening. Whether they use it is another matter. I won’t hold my breath.

item.title: What does COP31 reveal about the geopolitics of climate change?
item.description:
What does COP31 reveal about the geopolitics of climate change? Expert comment jon.wallace 19 November 2026

Some claim COPs take place in a bubble. But the summits say much about the interplay between climate policy, the energy transition, and the shifts underway in international relations.

Today, much of the political right in developed countries rejects efforts to combat climate change. Even leaders nominally of the centre and left are deprioritizing efforts to reduce emissions. Meanwhile many corporations are dropping their net zero targets. And fossil fuel companies are scrapping or scaling back their low-carbon divisions. 

It might seem strange, then, that this year’s COP31 climate change conference in Turkey attracted more people than ever. A record 93,000 participants as well as 77 heads of state and governments registered to attend. 

A COP headcount is a crude proxy for the global salience of climate policy. Nevertheless, it is worth asking: Is COP31 taking place in a bubble that is disconnected from geopolitical realities? Or does it indicate how climate change and the energy transition are simultaneously reflecting and influencing seismic geopolitical shifts?

Detached from reality?

When the first COP summit took place in Bonn in 1995, the world was vastly different. Climate-fuelled disasters were still theoretical. Practical, affordable low-carbon technology was a distant dream. The United States appeared to be the world’s only superpower, its alliances assured. 

Want to hear more on the path to a secure energy transition?

Join us at our climate and energy summit, where policymakers and industry leaders tackle the toughest questions on climate and energy security.

All of this has changed. Yet many negotiating positions at COP remain frozen in time. Entrenched definitions of ‘developed’ and ‘developing’ countries shape expectations of who is responsible for providing climate finance. 

That is despite some of the latter group – notably the Gulf states – now being amongst the world’s wealthiest on a per capita basis. Developing countries call for knowledge and technology transfer from developed countries, even though it is China – considered a developing country – that is overwhelmingly dominant in the field. 

Meanwhile the level of ambition seems at odds with the reality of an urgent, present climate crisis. For instance, the flagship electrification target proposed by hosts Australia and Turkey at COP31 will not require that the electricity generated must come from low carbon sources, despite the clear cost advantage in doing so. Such a stipulation is basically off the table in Antalya, a consequence of the continued influence of fossil fuel interests.

COPs do therefore, to some extent, take place in a bubble. But they are vital in understanding the interplay of climate change with real-world geopolitics.

‘Developed’ countries

The countries considered developed when the climate regime was established in the early 1990s are today on the back foot. In some, domestic consensus has eroded, making it more difficult for politicians and officials to negotiate climate change at the global level. 

The most extreme example is the United States. The US is not represented by a delegation at COP31, with President Donald Trump having formally withdrawn the country from the Paris Agreement in 2025 and the underlying UN convention in 2026. This followed a period of energetic US reengagement on international climate policy under President Joe Biden, following the US withdrawal from Paris in 2017 during President Trump’s first term.  

This whipsaw climate policy is influenced by the US’s superpower showdown with China. That competition would ideally encourage a ‘race-to-the-top’ on low-carbon technology, as it briefly did under President Biden with the Inflation Reduction Act. But policy is also influenced by the US’s newfound position as the world’s leading oil and gas producer. President Trump’s ‘energy dominance’ strategy has sought to capitalize on that position while dismissing climate science and rejecting renewable energy.

The EU, traditionally among the most ambitious of the blocs at COP, has dialled down its expectations for COP31 – in no small part due to the absence of the US. The EU’s top climate diplomat, Wopke Hoestra, called for a narrow focus on the electrification target, while dismissing any further talks on finance as ‘dead in the water’. 

Europe’s political class is also distracted, not least by the Russian threat. The World Leaders’ Summit in Antalya was relatively light on European leadership, most of whom attended a security-focused European Political Community meeting in Dublin instead. 

Canada and the UK, positioning themselves as responsible ‘middle powers’, issued a joint statement at COP31 affirming their commitment to climate finance goals and announcing new funding pledges. But this international positioning is paired with domestic retreat. Under Prime Minister Mark Carney, Canada has dismantled climate policies and committed public funds to new fossil fuel infrastructure. Under Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the UK has approved new drilling for gas and is considering weakening electric vehicle targets.

Burnham did attend the COP leaders’ summit. But in his address, he said that the consensus on climate had ‘gone’. This betrays a UK-centric perspective. Cross-party support for climate action has indeed collapsed in Westminster. But a record share of the global population (75 per cent) considers climate change a serious threat.

‘Developing’ countries

The countries considered developing within the international climate regime include varying economy sizes and climate vulnerabilities. But some broad trends exist among them.

First, many are treating the new low-carbon economy as a major growth and development opportunity. Countries in South-East Asia, sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and Latin America are rolling out renewables at a rate which will soon match or exceed that of their rich-world peers. Saudi Arabia, which has long blocked progress at COPs (and reprised this role in Antalya) used COP31 to announce a major wind and solar energy deal with hosts Turkey.

Secondly, developing countries intend to hold developed countries to their commitments, as the world experiences climate impacts with ever greater frequency and severity. Financing climate adaptation and compensating loss and damage is becoming central at the talks and were repeatedly referenced at the Leaders’ Summit. 

However, very few developed countries have renewed their financial pledges after they expired in 2025. That is despite previously pledging to lead efforts to scale up climate finance to $300 billion by 2035. 

China

And then there is Beijing. China is, by some distance, the country responsible for the largest share of greenhouse gas emissions (29.5 per cent in 2025). But it is also deploying low-carbon technologies at breathtaking speed and scale. 

Related work

What does China’s new Five-Year Plan mean for the climate?

It is exporting its solar panels, batteries, EVs and more, framing this as a central part of its contribution to global climate efforts. That is not without justification: the country’s clean tech exports in 2026 will cut emissions equivalent to what Brazil emits in a year. 

Here is where climate and geopolitics truly meet. Developed countries are struggling to honour their international climate finance commitments and decelerating their domestic efforts (or in the case of the US, repudiating both). Meanwhile, China, which styles itself as the leader of the developing countries, is supplying the means to transition, and providing huge investment in clean tech manufacturing abroad.

This is despite concerns that China is part of an effort, along with Saudi Arabia, Russia, India and Kenya, to delay work on crucial climate science. 

Separating the signal from the noise

When the COP process began in the 1990s, the goal was simple: to fix climate change. These days, very few would argue it can manage that on its own. 

When the dust settles, COP31 will have provided us with a distorted, confusing and ultimately dissatisfying representation of collective efforts to address climate change – as it always has. 

But focusing on conference outcomes alone ignores real world progress on the energy transition, and how climate change continues to shape and be shaped by geopolitical shifts. 

The Iran war has made low-carbon technology more attractive in many parts of the world. The traditional leaders of the Global North are seen by the Global South as reluctant to meet their commitments to tackle a climate crisis that is increasingly disruptive. China is receiving an ever-warmer reception, through its clean technology, its investments, and its relative stability as an international climate actor. 

COP31 may conclude this week, but the geopolitics of climate change and the energy transition are only getting started.

item.title: What the Nvidia Scandal Reveals About Modern Espionage
item.description:
Espionage is often called the world’s second-oldest profession. Its overlap with the first has now reached the frontier of artificial intelligence. Nvidia’s billionaire co-founder Jensen Huang, instantly recognisable by his shock of grey hair and trademark leather jacket, has resigned amid a scandal involving an affair with Alice Huang, a former Chinese television reporter turned businesswoman suspected by American intelligence of working for Beijing. The national security concern is a possible chain of influence: the Chinese Communist Party influencing Huang through her, and Huang influencing Donald Trump, whose administration eased restrictions on chip exports to China. That chain has not been established. China denies the allegations, and what, if anything, was compromised remains under investigation.

A crucial uncertainty remains: if Alice Huang was working for Chinese intelligence, we do not know whether she was planted to seduce him or recruited after an existing relationship offered an opportunity. Public reporting has not settled that chronology. Either possibility would explain the national security concerns, but only the first would establish that the relationship began as a deliberate honey trap. Nvidia, until recently the world’s most valuable company, supplies processors that underpin the AI revolution, giving access to its leadership strategic value far beyond its shareholders. History shows that honey traps can produce devastating intelligence losses, but getting someone into bed and running them as a dependable source are different achievements.

The Butterfly Effect

Chinese intelligence was responsible for one of the most extraordinary operations in espionage history. In Beijing in 1964, Bernard Boursicot, a twenty-year-old accountant at the French embassy, met the Chinese opera performer Shi Pei Pu. He was a junior embassy employee, far removed from the polished diplomat of spy fiction, whose desire for intimacy drew him into a story he proved willing to believe. Boursicot subsequently maintained that he believed Shi, a man, was a woman obliged to live publicly as a man. Their intermittent relationship continued for nearly two decades. According to Boursicot, their sexual encounters took place in darkness, which he attributed to modesty. Shi even presented a boy as their biological child. Boursicot passed French embassy documents to Chinese intelligence, explaining that he wanted to protect his lover. According to one study, a tip-off from Chinese intelligence source Yu Zhensan helped expose Boursicot. France’s counterintelligence service, the DST, investigated; Boursicot and Shi were arrested in Paris in 1983. Both were convicted of espionage in 1986. Their story inspired David Henry Hwang’s M. Butterfly, which overturns the Western romantic fantasies embodied in Puccini’s Madama Butterfly.

The affair demonstrated how affection, cultural assumptions and self-deception could combine to overcome judgment. More recently, Christine Fang, also known as Fang Fang, cultivated American politicians, including Eric Swalwell, a onetime presidential hopeful. FBI interview summaries released in August 2026 recorded Swalwell acknowledging several sexual encounters with her. Those records also said investigators found no evidence of a corrupt quid pro quo between Fang and Swalwell or his office, and had not established federal corruption offences by him. Intimacy does not itself prove betrayal. But knowing a politician’s ambitions, insecurities, friendships and private habits can have intelligence value before anyone hands over a classified document.

From Russia with Leverage

The Soviet services became masters of sexual entrapment, using female operatives known as “swallows” to lure targets into compromising encounters. MI5 files opened in 2022 illuminate the case of John Vassall, a clerk with a taste for a grander life: carefully dressed, socially ambitious and attracted to the company of people above him in Whitehall’s hierarchy. Posted to the British embassy in Moscow in 1954, he was drawn into a social circle cultivated by Soviet intelligence. At a party, he was plied with alcohol and photographed during sexual encounters with men. “I remember someone in the party taking photographs,” he recalled in his police statement of September 20, 1962. Vassall later said that the photographs made him feel sick. They became instruments of blackmail. Homosexual acts between men were criminal offences in both Britain and the Soviet Union; exposure threatened his career, reputation and freedom. British law and social prejudice helped strengthen the Soviet blackmailer’s hand.

What followed was a substantial betrayal of naval secrets. Vassall supplied material concerning radar, torpedoes, anti-submarine warfare and other British and allied defence information. His modest rank concealed valuable access: after returning to London, he worked in Naval Intelligence and the office of the Civil Lord of the Admiralty. The evidence recovered included fifteen rolls of film containing approximately 140 photographs from seventeen classified documents. These were the tangible proceeds recovered, rather than the entirety of what he had passed over the years. The Russians paid him, and what began with sexual blackmail developed into a continuing, remunerated relationship. His case illustrates how the reasons for spying can accumulate: fear opens the door, money helps keep it open.

His exposure came through intelligence from inside the Soviet system. Yuri Nosenko, a KGB counterintelligence officer who secretly began supplying information to the CIA in 1962 and defected in 1964, provided details that helped narrow the search to Vassall. MI5 placed him under surveillance and searched his Dolphin Square flat, discovering cameras and films. On September 12, officers watched him arrive at the Admiralty in a grey suit and green hat, carrying a document case, newspaper and rolled umbrella—the outward appearance of Whitehall respectability. They detained him as he left work that evening. Developed films contained copies of Top Secret documents, and Vassall confessed. The honey trap had succeeded for years. Intelligence from inside the Soviet system, followed by surveillance and physical evidence, brought it down.

The Trouble with Romeo

Dmitri Bystrolyotov made seduction part of a career spent becoming other people. Handsome, multilingual and an accomplished actor in everyday life, he was one of the Soviet “illegals”: intelligence officers operating abroad under assumed identities without diplomatic cover or immunity. A former sailor with an artist’s eye and a taste for adventure, he moved through interwar Europe, presenting whatever identity might open a door. His targets included a French embassy employee and the wife of a British official; his prizes included diplomatic codes and communications. He served the Soviet agencies preceding the KGB, helping establish techniques its officers would inherit. His loyalty offered no protection when Stalin’s terror turned inward: arrested in 1938, he spent years in prisons and labour camps.

The KGB’s British Romeo was John Symonds, a corrupt former Scotland Yard detective who fled prosecution and offered his services to Soviet intelligence in 1972. His retrospective recruitment slogan was memorable: “join the KGB, see the world—first class”. Dispatched to cultivate women with access to Western secrets, he slept with the wife of a West German government official, maintaining the affair through visits to Bonn; her intelligence was considered important enough for a personal report to KGB chairman Yuri Andropov. But Romeo’s charms had their limits. One British embassy target yielded little beyond gossip; another rejected him, his file recording that “his physical characteristics did not appeal” to her. Even the KGB could not make attraction a matter of state planning.

Honey traps can take almost infinite forms, but two broad approaches recur. The “negative” approach uses entrapment and the threat of exposure to compel cooperation. The “positive” approach cultivates affection and trust over time, sometimes through a relationship lasting years. Positive describes the inducement, rather than the ethics: the intimacy may be thoroughly deceptive. Netflix’s Black Doves offers a fictional version, with Keira Knightley’s character using her marriage to a politician to obtain his secrets.

East Germany’s Stasi turned this approach into its “secretaries’ offensives”, preying on lonely women whose access to classified material made them valuable targets. A secretary handling a minister’s papers could offer more useful access than a senior official. One early Romeo, codenamed Felix, was an engineering student persuaded to exchange his studies for espionage. In West Germany he waited near a bus stop used by chancellery staff and cultivated a secretary codenamed Norma. She fell in love and passed him secrets; he also developed feelings for her, and they lived together. When the Stasi learned that Felix was under suspicion, it recalled him. Norma returned from work to an empty apartment, unaware of his real identity or why he had vanished. The operation illustrates both the power of manufactured intimacy and the difficulty of controlling the emotions it creates.

Sometimes the trap backfires. The late Czech intelligence defector Larry Bittman once told me how his service tried to compromise an Italian politician visiting behind the Iron Curtain. The ingredients were familiar: sex, photographs and the expectation that embarrassment would secure cooperation. But when the politician was shown the photographs, he liked what he saw and asked for copies. What was intended as blackmail became a souvenir.

There are certainly examples of Western services exploiting sexual relationships, and no claim of Western innocence survives historical scrutiny. But British and American foreign-intelligence services have generally refrained from making honey traps a routine recruitment method. Former officers describe institutional reluctance and practical dangers. A source attached to one officer may refuse a replacement; a blackmailed source may become resentful, unreliable or willing to confess. CIA training actively discourages coercive recruitment for such reasons. We cannot judge the overall effectiveness of honey traps from spectacular successes alone: we do not know how many approaches went nowhere, or how many relationships produced nothing useful. A compromising photograph captures a moment. Running an agent requires years.

Western intelligence has also been accused of setting sexual traps. In 2023, a Chinese court sentenced the American citizen John Shing-Wan Leung to life imprisonment for espionage. China’s Ministry of State Security subsequently alleged that he helped American intelligence lure visiting Chinese officials into hotels equipped with surveillance devices, using sexual encounters as potential instruments of blackmail. The public court announcement disclosed no evidence about those alleged operations.

An Affair of State

Did Jensen Huang really need a honey trap to persuade him to sell to China? Hardly. Nvidia had an obvious commercial interest in gaining access to an enormous market.

The real scandal is the suspected diversion of advanced Nvidia chips to America’s chief rival in the AI race. US investigators are examining whether Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company, served as a front for getting chips subject to US export controls into China. Megaspeed denies illegally diverting chips. Who in Washington knew about the suspected diversion, when did they learn of it, and what did they do?

That makes the question more precise: did the relationship give Beijing privileged access, information or influence beyond what ordinary business interests would have delivered? Wanting to sell chips to China is not, by itself, evidence of manipulation.

The concern reaches into the White House: did Beijing influence Huang through Alice Huang, and did he then influence Trump to ease chip restrictions? The administration’s January 2026 change allowed case-by-case consideration of H200 exports to China. Congress should establish what the president knew, and when he knew it. Reporting describes a warning from Marco Rubio aboard Air Force One; Trump disputes knowing about the matter then. Did US intelligence warn Huang? Nvidia says he received no defensive briefing. If so, why not?

High IQ, Familiar Weaknesses

Silicon Valley is a principal intelligence target for China and other states. Its concentration of technology, capital and expertise gives privately held information enormous strategic value. It is full of highly intelligent, eccentric and often introverted people whose personal lives have not always been as successful as their professional careers. Professional success can make a flattering proposition seem less suspicious than overdue, encouraging them to look the other way when questions ought to be asked. For an intelligence service, the prize lies in the boardroom; the bedroom offers a route in. Chinese intelligence has repeatedly worked in concert with ostensibly independent Chinese companies, using commercial relationships, contractors and front organisations to acquire information.

We cannot yet prove this was a Chinese intelligence operation, but it bears familiar fingerprints: personal relationships and opaque corporate vehicles. Megaspeed’s reported Singapore office was sparsely staffed or practically empty, its ownership passed through an offshore vehicle to the newly incorporated Swiftdata, and its assets jumped from $33 million in 2023 to about $3 billion in 2024. Who controlled and financed it? Megaspeed denies illicit chip transfers.

The alleged smuggling involved some of the world’s most powerful AI hardware. According to The Information, in reporting carried by Reuters, Alice Huang helped a corporate network move roughly 240,000 Nvidia H100, H200 and older A100 processors into China, worth at least $7.5 billion. These chips train and run AI models with civilian and military applications—the capabilities Washington’s export controls seek to keep from Beijing.

Honey traps have as many variations as human frailties. Desire, loneliness, fear, ambition and vanity can each provide an opening. A high IQ is no defense against a flattering proposition. History has a warning for the tech bros: if it seems too good to be true, it probably is.

Washington Should Allow Ukraine to Hit Russia's Ballistic Missile Launchers
item.description:
Earlier this month I traveled to Ukraine and met with soldiers, corps commanders, and business leaders in Kyiv, Dnipro, Pavlohrad, and Kharkiv. I was in Kyiv on November 7 when Russia launched 36 ballistic missiles overnight toward the capital and the region around it. Ukrainian air defenses stopped four. The attack was aimed mainly at energy infrastructure, three days before negotiators met in Abu Dhabi.

I want to make the case for allowing Ukraine to hit the launchers that fire these missiles. What Ukraine needs is a White House approval, not a new weapon: permission to use Starshield, SpaceX's satellite service for military customers, as far as 300 kilometers into Russia and only against ballistic missile launchers. This is good for the United States. It would put pressure on Russia to negotiate seriously, there is no cost to us, and it is not complex.

The problem

Russia strikes Kyiv and Dnipro with its own Iskander ballistic missiles and with North Korean KN-23s. It fires them from mobile launchers spread across four regions: Voronezh, Kursk, Oryol, and Bryansk. Ukrainian officers put the number of launchers at about 65. A launcher typically stays at its firing position for only a few minutes before it relocates.

Ukraine does not have enough interceptors to stop these missiles. President Zelensky said on October 27 that Ukraine has received an average of 12 Patriot interceptors a month from the United States this year.

Ukraine began going after the launchers in May. Its officers describe the results so far as limited: some launchers damaged, few destroyed. They say Ukraine can now locate the launchers in most cases. What it cannot do is get a large enough warhead to them before they move. The drones Ukraine sends that far into Russia are controlled through radio relays and carry small payloads, so a hit usually damages a launcher without destroying it. Ukraine's bigger drones, with payloads of up to about 200 kilograms, fly on a Starshield link, which Ukraine has over occupied territory but not inside Russia.

If Starshield were available to Ukraine across a strip of Russian territory extending roughly 300 kilometers from the border, the officers believe they could destroy the majority of the launchers in it or force Russia to pull them back. In their judgment, Russia's ground-launched ballistic missiles would then no longer reach Kyiv, Dnipro, or the power plants of central Ukraine. Kharkiv would probably remain within range, and missiles launched from aircraft would not be affected. I cannot verify this estimate, but it comes from officers who have spent six months trying to hit these launchers.

Why this is good for the United States

Ukraine's army is holding the front, and the commanders I met expect to keep holding it. Russia has not been able to break through on the battlefield, so it is putting pressure on Ukraine's civilians instead. During my visit, some households in Kyiv without a generator were down to two hours of electricity per day. Russia is terrorizing civilians to pressure Ukraine's government, and ballistic missiles are the part of that campaign Ukraine has the hardest time stopping. On November 7, Ukraine stopped 149 of 172 drones but only four of 36 ballistic missiles.

The Kyiv Independent reported on November 18 that the Kremlin believes it has the advantage in the talks. It pointed to two factors: Russia's strikes on Ukraine's energy system continue, and Ukraine is struggling to get enough interceptors. It also said the Russian delegation in Abu Dhabi showed little interest in an energy ceasefire. The talks produced an agreement in principle on a prisoner exchange, but no breakthrough on a ceasefire or on territory.

If Ukraine can destroy the launchers or push them out of range, Russia loses much of its ability to hit Kyiv and Dnipro with ballistic missiles. That removes much of the pressure on civilians that Russia is counting on. Without it, Russia has less reason to believe it can win by waiting and more reason to negotiate seriously. I cannot say for certain that Russia would then agree to a settlement, but it has little reason to compromise while these attacks are working. Some have argued that allowing these strikes would not help end the war. I think the opposite is true.

Every launcher destroyed also means fewer missiles to intercept, at a time when we are short of interceptors ourselves. CSIS estimates that the war with Iran used up about half of our Patriot interceptors.

What it would take from Washington

There is no cost to the United States. Ukraine builds the drones and flies them, so no American weapons, interceptors, or new funding are needed.

It is also not complex. Ukraine already uses Starshield on its strike drones over occupied Ukraine, and the service ends at the Russian border. Ukraine reports that a speed limit has interfered with those flights this month; SpaceX says it has imposed none. The service is already controlled by terminal and by location, so letting registered Ukrainian terminals work 300 kilometers into Russia is a change to settings that have been changed before.

The decision belongs to the White House. Elon Musk has said that the U.S. government owns and controls Starshield, and that the U.S. military and ultimately the president decide the limits on its use.

The approval can be narrow: ballistic missile launchers only. This autumn, Washington objected to Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries, and refineries would not be covered. Ukrainian officers say each terminal is registered individually, and that inside this strip they would move their strikes away from economic targets and onto military ones.

The White House should make this decision now. Ukrainian officers say Russia already protects some of its fixed sites with satellite jamming and is likely to have mobile jammers in a few months. Approving it would help protect civilians in Kyiv and Dnipro this winter, at no cost to the United States, and would give Russia a real reason to negotiate.

item.title: Will Saddam Haftar be Libya’s next president?
item.description:
Will Saddam Haftar be Libya’s next president? Expert comment thilton.drupal 20 November 2026

The son of commander Khalifa Haftar has consolidated his position as heir apparent and expanded his influence. But his pursuit of the presidency could bring Libya back into conflict.

Saddam Haftar, the son of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF) commander Khalifa Haftar, has recently visited several foreign capitals in an apparent attempt to boost his international standing. This has been seen as part of a concerted push to become Libya’s next president.

This effort will define Libya’s politics for the coming months. It has huge implications for the country’s political future amid a US-led push for a national government that would unify Libya’s two rival administrations: the LAAF-controlled administration in eastern Libya and the Government of National Unity (GNU) in Tripoli. Strong opposition to Saddam’s goals in western Libya also means that the risk of conflict is increasing.

Saddam becomes heir apparent

For many years, there have been questions over Khalifa Haftar’s succession. The assumption has been that Haftar, 83, would remain in direct control of the LAAF while alive. It was speculated that the LAAF could fragment without Haftar, given the LAAF’s status as a hybrid of a military institution and a family enterprise.  

However, in recent years, Haftar has increasingly taken a back seat as his sons Saddam, Khaled, Belgassim and al-Sadiq have come to the fore. Their rise became clearer after the failure of the LAAF to capture Tripoli in 2020, which led Haftar to reassess his approach. Over subsequent years, the LAAF was restructured. Its forces were placed under the command of Saddam and Khaled, who gained responsibility for land forces and security units respectively. 

Meanwhile, Belgassim developed strong networks and influence in political circles. He was instrumental in the formation of a new government that sought to replace the sitting GNU in Tripoli. In 2023, Belgassim also assumed the helm of the Libyan Development and Reconstruction Programme, formed after floods killed several thousand people in Derna, which provided a new narrative of development for the Haftar family.

However, Khalifa’s appointment of Saddam as deputy general commander in August 2025 sealed his position as heir apparent. Saddam has become the most powerful of the sons through not just his military position, but also his alleged increasing influence via proxies over the oil and gas and banking sectors in eastern Libya.

The Boulos initiative

Saddam’s rise is important in the context of the push for a unified government in Libya. This has been led by Massad Boulos, the US Special Advisor for Africa and the Middle East. Under Boulos’ plan, a unified government would be formed as part of a deal between the two ruling families: the Haftars, who control eastern Libya, and the Dabaibas, who control the Tripoli-based GNU.

While the US has not publicized the parameters of the deal, insiders have said that Saddam Haftar would become a member of the Presidency Council, the three-person body whose chairman is Libya’s de facto head of state. The Dabaiba family would retain the prime minister’s post.

Related work

Why US plans for power-sharing in Libya will not work

Negotiating processes had previously focused on seeking agreement between Libya’s fractious institutions: the chronically divided House of Representatives in eastern Libya and the Tripoli-based High State Council. But the US plan has broken with this formula, instead seeking agreement between the Haftars and the Dabaibas. The first agreement made through this channel was a deal on budgetary spending in April 2026.

Subsequently, the United Nations adapted to the new format. The UN Mission’s ‘4+4’ committee brought together a combination of representatives from the GNU, LAAF, the House of Representatives and the High State Council. The 4+4 reached agreement on a roadmap for national elections in August.

This pivot towards negotiations being between the LAAF and the GNU – essentially between the emissaries of Saddam Haftar and the Dabaibas – is more significant than the content of the agreement. It officially places Saddam’s LAAF General Command as a negotiating party with parity with the internationally recognized GNU.  

Path to the presidency?

Buoyed by these diplomatic advances, Saddam has recently made significant moves to expand his influence.

The ousting of the longtime speaker of the House of Representatives in October – and his replacement with a figure known for his support for the LAAF – is widely understood to have been orchestrated by Saddam.

Shortly after, the House of Representatives moved to ratify a controversial memorandum of understanding with Turkey over the recognition of drilling rights in the eastern Mediterranean. Insiders have said privately that Saddam pushed for this move, which angered Egypt and European countries, presumably with the aim of securing Ankara’s support for his push for the presidency in return.

Then, on 26 October, the governor of the Central Bank of Libya was replaced, reportedly due to a private agreement between the Haftars and the Dabaibas. The Central Bank holds a critical place in the management of Libya’s economy, overseeing the distribution of foreign currency and dinar payments that are so crucial to Libya’s leaders.

That same week, Saddam was in Turkey for talks with the GNU on military reunification.

Alongside strengthening his influence over important institutions in Libya, Saddam has consequently emerged as the apparent partner of preference for the some of the most influential international actors. He is seen as someone who can get things done and maintain order in comparison to the messy picture of contested power in western Libya.

The enduring Haftar ‘problem’ and the risk of conflict

Saddam is now central to any political effort to reunify the country. His ambitions to enter Tripoli are widely known. Those familiar with the security sector in the capital note that local allies of Saddam are seeking to prepare the ground for his arrival.

But opposition to – and mistrust of – Saddam in western Libya remains strong, especially in key constituencies such as the city of Misrata. This has not been helped by the uncovering of a sleeper cell, allegedly linked to the LAAF, that was accused of seeking to cause damage to oil and gas infrastructure in the city of Zawiya in August.

Many doubt that Saddam is willing to share power. It therefore seems no meaningful guarantees can be provided to Saddam’s opponents to reassure them. Western Libyan actors would like to separate the discussion of military reunification from political reunification as a result.

Consequently, while the Dabaiba family may be willing to cut deals to retain a modus vivendi with Saddam, it is highly unlikely to sign a deal making Saddam president. This is evident in the fact that no deal has yet been reached, despite intensive efforts over months by Boulos.

This, in turn, creates a problem. It is not clear how Saddam’s rapid rise and apparent aspirations for president can be squared with his opponents’ steadfast opposition to him. And they are unlikely to go anywhere, considering that the Dabaibas are entrenched in power too.

This fundamental difference runs deeper than the Boulos initiative. As one source in the security sector told me: even if there were elections, Saddam would not accept the results if he loses, and his opponents would not accept the results if he wins.

If Saddam continues to push for the presidency, Libya therefore faces a heightened risk of conflict. Many of his opponents would seemingly prefer the messy situation in Tripoli to prevail over a new order that could ultimately end up squarely under Saddam’s control. But, given the strength of international support building behind Saddam’s campaign, their options are narrowing.

item.title: The ICJ’s Myanmar finding shifts the dial – a little – on the grounds for a guilty verdict in a genocide case
item.description:
The ICJ’s Myanmar finding shifts the dial – a little – on the grounds for a guilty verdict in a genocide case Expert comment jon.wallace 20 November 2026

The Court’s unusually split decision seems to adjust how intent to destroy a group ‘in whole or in part’ is established.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the highest court in the world, has ruled that Myanmar is guilty of genocide. According to the Court, the ‘clearance’ campaign by the Myanmar military against its Rohingya minority of 2017 was aimed at the destruction, in whole or in part, of that community. The finding in this case, which was brought before the Court by the Gambia in 2019, will reverberate far beyond Myanmar and its immediate environment.

The ICJ’s previous genocide cases

The Rohingya are a mainly Muslim ethnic group that has been excluded from Myanmar citizenship and discriminated against for decades. In the wake of attacks by terrorist groups against the military in 2016, some 10,000 Rohingya were killed, and over 85 per cent of its population of around 850,000 were displaced from Myanmar over the following year in a campaign of killings, rape and the burning of villages.

Hear directly from the experts

Get nuanced insights from Chatham House experts on the issues shaping the global policy and geopolitical landscape.

The ICJ has established a very high bar for confirming that genocide has occurred. Several cases, including those brought by Croatia against Serbia and Sudan against the UAE, have been unsuccessful. 

Others are still ongoing, addressing the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Rwanda, Ukraine and the Russian Federation, and Gaza.

Only once before, in relation to the 1995 Srebrenica massacre of 8,000 men and boys in Bosnia and Herzegovina, has the ICJ confirmed genocide. But controversially, it failed to attribute the atrocity to its alleged author, the Republic of Serbia (then the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia) under Slobodan Milosevic.

This new decision of the Court moves the dial ever so slightly, reducing the legal hurdles on the way towards a finding of genocide. 

The grounds for a finding of genocide

According to the Genocide Convention of 1948, genocide requires three elements. 

First, it must be directed against a protected group, defined by national, ethnic, racial or religious characteristics. Second, there must be prohibited acts directed against members of the group. This includes killings, causing serious bodily or mental harm, inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about the destruction of the group, or measures intended to prevent births or forcibly transferring children to another group. 

But critically, even if a pattern of such practices is clearly evident, this must be carried by the specific intent to destroy the group as such ‘in whole or in part’ – the third element.

This may seem odd. If the result is the destruction of the group, one might argue that this should suffice to constitute genocide. Such conduct would clearly amount to a crime against humanity and other severe violations of human rights and humanitarian law. However, in defining what is sometimes called ‘the crime of crimes,’ the Genocide Convention imposes this additional criterion of specific intent. 

Of course, that is difficult to prove. States no longer record their decision to commit genocide in a formal document, as Hitler’s government did in the famous 1942 Wannsee Protocol, which planned the complete destruction of Europe’s Jewish population. 

Without such formal documentation, proof of the intent to destroy a group in whole or in part must be inferred from the nature of a systematic campaign of killing and other acts proscribed by the Genocide Convention that are directed at a defined population segment.

Previously, the Court asserted that such an inference can only be made if this pattern cannot be explained by any reason other than the intention to commit genocide. 

In its defence, Myanmar offered several alternative grounds to explain the nature of its armed campaign. It referred to the need to mount a counter-terrorism effort following attacks by rebel movements in Rakhine province, where most Rohingya used to reside. However, in view of the Court, this motivation would not explain the pattern of brutal attacks against the civilian population.

The Court also considered whether Myanmar’s conduct might simply have been directed at the forcible displacement of the Rohingya, rather than their destruction in whole or in part. This alone would be a serious international crime, but it would not quite amount to genocide.

However, the Court looked at the overall context of the long-standing campaign against the Rohingya – including discrimination, hate speech, the nature of the military operation and other culpable acts systematically targeting this group and affecting its ‘foundations’ or existence.

In broadening this overall context, and relying on the totality of the evidence, rather than just the well attested reports of individual atrocities, the Court was able to assert that the intent to commit genocide was the only reasonable inference that could be drawn.

The effect on other cases

This outcome will concern some governments involved in other ongoing cases regarding genocide. 

Ukraine brought a case before the ICJ in 2022, asking the Court to confirm that it had not committed genocide against Russian-speakers on its territory – a central claim made by Russia to justify its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that year. 

In another case, the DRC is alleging that Rwanda is involved in genocide conducted on its territory. In a further action, Nicaragua is alleging that Germany shares responsibility for the alleged genocide in Gaza due to its supply of arms to Israel. 

The Court’s Myanmar judgement may impact these cases. But international attention is mainly focused on the case’s implications for South Africa’s genocide case against Israel. 

In an initial, provisional phase of the case, the Court found that there may be a plausible case of genocide in relation to Israel’s military campaign in Gaza.

Counsel for Israel and South Africa, along with the over 20 others states that have intervened in that case, will now assess the Court’s finding and ask: what would the outcome be if the matrix of factors applied by the ICJ in the Myanmar case were applied to Israel’s armed campaign in Gaza? Would this exercise demonstrate that the intent to commit genocide is the only reasonable explanation for the character of that campaign?

Related work

South Africa’s genocide case against Israel: The International Court of Justice explained

The key clauses in the Myanmar judgement were adopted by an unusually divided Court, by a majority of 9 to 6. The ICJ decides according to the applicable law, not the politics involved in a given situation. But its decision will probably be criticized by some as having lowered the threshold for the identification of genocide, perhaps with a view to confirming the relevance of the Court and of the international rule of law. International law has been largely disregarded in many recent conflicts – especially its humanitarian provisions. 

On the other hand, those opposing the Court’s finding might be accused of trying to prevent a precedent being established when it comes to evaluating the Gaza case.

In addition to political controversy, the case raises another important issue: A third state, The Gambia – which is not involved in Myanmar’s conflict – managed to obtain a ruling in favour of a dispossessed and internationally disenfranchised minority group located a continent away. 

The Gambia brought the action with the support of the Organization of the Islamic Conference and senior international lawyers, adopting a kind of international public service role in defence of the international public order. It confirmed that all states have a firm legal interest in compliance with that rule by all other states, and that parties to the Genocide Convention can bring a case to the Court in defence of the prohibition of genocide. 

The Court even considered that in this case between The Gambia and Myanmar, it has the authority to rule on the entitlement of the Rohingya as the ultimate beneficiaries of the obligation to prevent genocide to restitution and compensation from their own government. In this way, it has reasserted and indeed extended its role of guardian of the international rule of law at a time of challenge to global order.
